title: Docker Complete Notes
summary: A full study-notes series on Docker: how images and containers work under the hood, writing Dockerfiles, persisting data with volumes, container networking, multi-service apps with Compose, publishing to registries, and production best practices.

chapters.title: Docker Complete Notes
points: Docker: platform to build, ship and run applications in containers
Series covers: images, containers, Dockerfile, volumes, networking, Compose, registry, best practices
Why it matters: 'works on my machine' solved by shipping the environment with the app
Prerequisites: basic Linux shell, some idea of processes and ports

chapters.title: What Docker Is and Why It Exists
points: Definition: Docker packages an app plus its dependencies into a container that runs the same on any host with a Docker engine
Problem it solves: dependency drift between dev, test and prod; 'works on my machine'
Container = isolated process (or process group) sharing the host kernel, not a full OS
Three core nouns: image (blueprint), container (running instance), registry (image store)
Docker Engine parts: dockerd daemon, REST API, docker CLI client; CLI talks to daemon over a Unix socket or TCP
containerd and runc: Docker delegates container lifecycle to containerd, which uses runc (OCI runtime) to actually start the process
OCI (Open Container Initiative) standardizes image format and runtime, so Docker images run on Podman, Kubernetes, etc
Container vs VM: VM virtualizes hardware and boots a guest kernel (GBs, minutes); container shares kernel (MBs, milliseconds)
Typical flow: write Dockerfile, docker build, docker run, docker push to registry, docker pull elsewhere
Mistake: treating a container like a VM and running many services plus SSH inside it
Summary: Docker = standardized, portable, lightweight process isolation with a shipping format

chapters.title: Container Internals: Namespaces, cgroups, Union FS
points: Linux namespaces give each container its own view: pid (process tree), net (interfaces, ports), mnt (filesystem mounts), uts (hostname), ipc (shared memory), user (uid mapping)
PID namespace: container's main process is PID 1 inside, but a normal PID on the host; ps on host shows it
cgroups (control groups) limit and account resources: CPU shares, memory cap, block IO, pids count
docker run --memory=512m --cpus=1.5 sets cgroup limits; exceeding memory limit triggers OOM kill of the container
Union / overlay filesystem (overlay2): image layers stacked read-only, plus one thin writable container layer on top
Copy-on-write: modifying a file from a lower layer copies it up into the writable layer first
Capabilities: containers drop most root capabilities by default (no CAP_SYS_ADMIN); --cap-add / --cap-drop adjust
Seccomp and AppArmor profiles filter syscalls the container may make
PID 1 problem: if your app is PID 1 it must reap zombies and handle SIGTERM; use --init or tini
Docker Desktop on Mac/Windows runs a Linux VM under the hood; containers are still Linux processes there
Mistake: assuming container isolation equals VM security; kernel is shared, kernel exploits escape
Summary: container = namespaces (isolation) + cgroups (limits) + overlay layers (filesystem)

chapters.title: Images and Layers
points: Image: immutable, read-only template made of ordered layers plus a JSON config (entrypoint, env, exposed ports)
Each layer is a tarball of filesystem diffs, content-addressed by SHA256 digest
Image name anatomy: registry/namespace/repo:tag, e.g. docker.io/library/nginx:1.27; default registry Docker Hub, default tag latest
Tag vs digest: tag is a mutable pointer; digest (nginx@sha256:...) is immutable and reproducible
latest is not 'newest', just the tag used when none given; pinning versions avoids surprise upgrades
Layer sharing: two images built from the same base share those layers on disk and in the registry
docker images / docker image ls lists local images; docker image inspect shows config and layer digests
docker history <image> shows each layer, its size and the instruction that created it
docker pull downloads only layers not already present; docker push uploads only missing layers
docker rmi removes an image; dangling images (<none>) are untagged leftovers; docker image prune cleans them
docker save / docker load export and import an image as a tar for offline transfer
Multi-arch images: a manifest list maps one tag to per-platform images (amd64, arm64); docker buildx builds them
Mistake: docker rmi failing because a stopped container still references the image
Summary: image = stack of content-addressed layers + config; tags point, digests pin

chapters.title: Container Lifecycle and Core Commands
points: Container: a runnable instance of an image with its own writable layer, network namespace and process
States: created, running, paused, stopped (exited), removed; docker ps shows running, docker ps -a shows all
docker run = docker create + docker start; docker run -d detaches, -it gives an interactive TTY
docker run --name web -p 8080:80 nginx maps host port 8080 to container port 80
docker run --rm deletes the container on exit; useful for one-off commands
docker stop sends SIGTERM, waits 10s (configurable with -t), then SIGKILL; docker kill sends SIGKILL at once
docker exec -it web sh opens a shell in a running container; docker attach connects to PID 1's stdio
docker logs -f web streams stdout/stderr; logs are captured only from PID 1's stdout and stderr
docker inspect returns full JSON: IP, mounts, env, restart policy; use --format '{{.NetworkSettings.IPAddress}}'
docker cp copies files between host and container; docker stats shows live CPU and memory usage
Restart policies: no, on-failure[:n], always, unless-stopped; set with --restart
Exit code semantics: 0 success, 137 = killed by SIGKILL (often OOM), 143 = SIGTERM
docker container prune removes all stopped containers; docker system prune removes containers, networks, dangling images
Mistake: running docker run repeatedly creates new containers each time instead of restarting the old one
Mistake: app ignores SIGTERM, so every stop takes 10 seconds then a hard kill

chapters.title: Dockerfile Fundamentals
points: Dockerfile: text recipe of instructions; docker build executes them top to bottom to produce an image
FROM sets the base image; must be first (except ARG before FROM); FROM scratch means an empty base
RUN executes a command at build time and commits a new layer; shell form (RUN apt-get ...) vs exec form (RUN ["apt-get", ...])
COPY copies files from build context into the image; ADD also unpacks local tars and fetches URLs (prefer COPY)
WORKDIR sets the working directory for following instructions and the container; creates it if missing
ENV sets persistent environment variables; ARG sets build-time-only variables passed with --build-arg
EXPOSE documents the port the app listens on; it does not publish anything, -p does
CMD provides the default command, overridable by docker run args; ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable, CMD becomes its args
USER switches to a non-root user for later instructions and runtime; create it with RUN adduser first
LABEL adds metadata; HEALTHCHECK defines a command Docker runs to mark the container healthy or unhealthy
Example: FROM python:3.12-slim / WORKDIR /app / COPY requirements.txt . / RUN pip install -r requirements.txt / COPY . . / CMD ["python", "app.py"]
.dockerignore excludes files (node_modules, .git, secrets) from the build context sent to the daemon
docker build -t myapp:1.0 . where the dot is the build context; -f picks a Dockerfile in another location
Mistake: using shell-form CMD so the app runs under /bin/sh -c and never receives SIGTERM directly

chapters.title: Build Cache, Layers and Multi-Stage Builds
points: Every RUN, COPY and ADD creates a layer; the build cache reuses a layer when the instruction and its inputs are unchanged
Cache invalidation is top-down: once one instruction misses, every instruction after it rebuilds
Order instructions from least to most frequently changing: base, system packages, dependency manifests, dependency install, source code
COPY package.json first, RUN npm install, then COPY . . so a source edit does not reinstall dependencies
Chain commands in one RUN with && and clean up in the same layer (rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*); a later RUN rm does not shrink earlier layers
Deleted files in later layers still exist in earlier ones; secrets copied then removed are still in the image
Multi-stage build: several FROM stages; the final stage copies only artifacts from earlier ones with COPY --from=builder
Example: FROM golang:1.23 AS builder / RUN go build -o app / FROM alpine / COPY --from=builder /src/app /app / ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
Result: build tools and source stay out of the final image; Go images drop from ~800MB to ~15MB
docker build --target builder stops at a named stage, handy for running tests in the build stage
BuildKit (default now): parallel stages, RUN --mount=type=cache for package caches, RUN --mount=type=secret for build secrets that never hit a layer
--no-cache forces a full rebuild; docker builder prune clears the build cache
Base image choice: full (debian) vs slim vs alpine (musl, smaller, some compat issues) vs distroless (no shell)
Mistake: COPY . . before dependency install, so every code change reinstalls everything

chapters.title: Volumes and Persistent Data
points: Container writable layer is ephemeral: removing the container deletes its data; volumes live outside that layer
Named volume: managed by Docker under /var/lib/docker/volumes; docker volume create data; -v data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
Bind mount: maps a host path into the container; -v $(pwd)/src:/app/src or --mount type=bind,src=...,dst=...
tmpfs mount: in-memory only, gone on stop; --tmpfs /run for secrets or scratch space
-v vs --mount: same result, --mount is explicit key=value and errors on a missing host path instead of creating a directory
Named volume vs bind mount: volumes are portable, backed up with docker tools, and work the same on every OS; bind mounts are for live code in dev
First mount of an empty named volume copies the image's existing files at that path into it; bind mounts hide the image's files
Read-only mounts: -v config:/etc/app:ro prevents the container from writing
docker volume ls, inspect, rm; docker volume prune removes unused volumes (data loss, check first)
Anonymous volumes: VOLUME instruction in Dockerfile or -v /data with no name; hard to track, pile up unless --rm -v
Backup pattern: docker run --rm -v data:/from -v $(pwd):/to alpine tar czf /to/backup.tgz -C /from .
Permissions: files created by container root are owned by root on the host with bind mounts; match uid with USER or chown
Volume drivers allow NFS, cloud block storage or other backends via --driver
Mistake: storing the database inside the container layer, then losing it on docker rm or image upgrade

chapters.title: Container Networking
points: Each container gets its own network namespace: own interfaces, IP, routing table and port space
Default bridge network (docker0): containers get private IPs (172.17.x.x), reach the internet via NAT, but only resolve each other by IP
User-defined bridge: docker network create appnet; containers on it resolve each other by container name via Docker's embedded DNS (127.0.0.11)
Port publishing: -p hostPort:containerPort adds an iptables DNAT rule; -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 restricts to localhost; -P publishes all EXPOSEd ports on random host ports
host network: --network host shares the host's network stack, no isolation, no port mapping needed (Linux only)
none network: --network none gives only loopback, for fully isolated jobs
overlay network: spans multiple Docker hosts (Swarm), encapsulates traffic in VXLAN
macvlan: container gets its own MAC and IP on the physical LAN, appears as a separate device
Container-to-container on the same user-defined network talk directly on container ports; published ports are only for outside access
host.docker.internal resolves to the host from inside a container (Desktop; on Linux add --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway)
docker network ls, inspect, connect, disconnect; a container can be on several networks at once
Network aliases: --network-alias db lets several containers answer to one name
Comparison: bridge (default, NAT, isolated) vs host (fast, no isolation) vs overlay (multi-host) vs none
Mistake: using localhost inside a container to reach another container; localhost is the container's own loopback
Mistake: binding the app to 127.0.0.1 inside the container, so published ports connect but get refused; bind 0.0.0.0

chapters.title: Docker Compose: Multi-Container Apps
points: Compose: define a multi-service application in one YAML file and manage it as a unit with docker compose (v2 plugin, replaces docker-compose v1)
Top-level keys: services, networks, volumes, configs, secrets; the version key is obsolete and ignored
Each service maps to one or more containers; keys include image or build, ports, environment, env_file, volumes, networks, depends_on, command, restart, healthcheck
Example: services: web: build: . ports: ['8000:8000'] depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy; db: image: postgres:16 volumes: ['pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data']; volumes: pgdata: {}
Compose creates a default network named <project>_default; services reach each other by service name (web connects to db:5432)
Project name comes from the directory name or -p; it prefixes containers, networks and volumes
docker compose up -d builds missing images, creates networks and volumes, starts services; docker compose down stops and removes containers and networks (add -v to remove volumes)
docker compose logs -f web, ps, exec web sh, build, pull, restart, stop, config (renders the resolved file)
depends_on only orders startup; use condition: service_healthy with a healthcheck to wait until the dependency is ready
Variable substitution: ${DB_PASSWORD} read from the shell or a .env file next to the compose file; ${VAR:-default} for fallbacks
Override files: docker-compose.override.yml is merged automatically; -f base.yml -f prod.yml stacks files for environments
Profiles: profiles: [debug] on a service, started only with --profile debug
Scaling: docker compose up --scale worker=3 runs multiple replicas of a stateless service (no fixed container_name or host port)
Compose vs Swarm/Kubernetes: Compose is single-host dev and small deployments; orchestration adds scheduling, self-healing and rolling updates
Mistake: expecting depends_on to wait for the database to accept connections; it only waits for the container to start

chapters.title: Registries: Storing and Sharing Images
points: Registry: HTTP service that stores and serves image layers and manifests; repository is one named image with many tags
Docker Hub is the default public registry; others: GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io), AWS ECR, Google Artifact Registry, Azure ACR, GitLab registry
Official images (library/nginx) are curated by Docker; verified publisher images are vendor-maintained; everything else is community and needs vetting
docker login registry.example.com stores credentials in ~/.docker/config.json (use a credential helper in production)
Push flow: docker tag myapp:1.0 ghcr.io/org/myapp:1.0 then docker push ghcr.io/org/myapp:1.0; the tag encodes the destination
Pull flow: docker pull ghcr.io/org/myapp:1.0; docker run pulls automatically if the image is missing
Only changed layers are transferred; the registry deduplicates layers across repositories by digest
Self-hosted registry: docker run -d -p 5000:5000 registry:2; insecure (HTTP) registries must be listed in daemon.json
Tagging strategy: semantic version (1.4.2), plus major (1.4, 1), plus git SHA for traceability; never rely on latest for deployments
Pull by digest (image@sha256:...) for immutable deployments; docker image inspect shows RepoDigests
Docker Hub rate limits anonymous and free pulls; mirrors or authenticated pulls avoid CI failures
Image signing and scanning: Docker Scout / Trivy scan for CVEs; cosign or Docker Content Trust sign images
Cleanup: registries keep old tags forever unless lifecycle policies (ECR) or garbage collection (registry:2) are configured
Mistake: pushing images that contain .env files or private keys copied in via COPY . . without a .dockerignore

chapters.title: Security and Resource Limits
points: Run as non-root: USER app in the Dockerfile; root in the container is root on the host if isolation breaks
Rootless Docker mode runs the daemon itself without root, at the cost of some features (no privileged ports, slower networking)
Never use --privileged in production; it grants all capabilities and device access, effectively host root
Drop capabilities: --cap-drop=ALL --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE keeps only what the app needs
--read-only filesystem plus --tmpfs for writable dirs stops attackers from persisting changes
Mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container gives it full control of the host's Docker; treat as root access
Secrets: never ENV or ARG secrets into images (visible in docker history); use runtime env from a secret store, Docker secrets, or BuildKit --mount=type=secret
Pin base images to specific versions or digests and rebuild regularly to pick up security patches
Scan images (docker scout cves, trivy image) in CI and fail on critical vulnerabilities
Resource limits: --memory 512m --memory-swap 512m (no swap), --cpus 1, --pids-limit 100 to prevent fork bombs
Without a memory limit a container can consume all host RAM; the kernel OOM killer may kill something else
Logging: default json-file driver grows unbounded; set --log-opt max-size=10m max-file=3 or use a log driver
Minimal images (slim, alpine, distroless) reduce attack surface and CVE count; no shell means no easy exec for attackers
Mistake: running as root with the Docker socket mounted, a full host compromise waiting for one app bug

chapters.title: Best Practices and Common Mistakes
points: One process per container: web, worker, db as separate containers; compose or an orchestrator wires them together
Immutable images: configuration through environment variables and mounted config, never docker exec edits that vanish on restart
Twelve-factor logging: write to stdout/stderr, let Docker capture; no log files inside the container
Handle SIGTERM for graceful shutdown; use exec-form ENTRYPOINT and --init or tini so signals reach the app
Add a HEALTHCHECK so orchestrators and compose depends_on can tell 'started' from 'ready'
Keep images small: multi-stage builds, slim bases, .dockerignore, clean package caches in the same RUN layer
Order Dockerfile for cache hits: dependencies before source; pin versions in package manifests for reproducible builds
Tag with version and git SHA; deploy by digest; never deploy latest
Persist state only in named volumes or external services; containers should be safe to delete any time
Use user-defined networks and service names instead of hard-coded IPs or --link (deprecated)
Dev vs prod: bind mounts and hot reload in dev via compose override; baked-in code and read-only filesystem in prod
Housekeeping: docker system df shows disk use; docker system prune -a --volumes reclaims space (destroys unused data, check first)
Common mistake: latest tag drift breaks builds months later when the base image changes
Common mistake: building on an arm64 Mac and deploying to amd64 servers without --platform, causing exec format error
Common mistake: huge build context because .git or node_modules is not in .dockerignore, making builds slow
Common mistake: exposing the Docker daemon on TCP 2375 without TLS; it is unauthenticated root access to the host

chapters.title: Docker Cheatsheet
points: Images: docker build -t name:tag . | docker images | docker pull img | docker push img | docker rmi img | docker history img | docker image prune
Containers: docker run -d --name c -p 8080:80 img | docker ps -a | docker stop c | docker start c | docker rm -f c | docker logs -f c | docker exec -it c sh | docker inspect c | docker stats
Run flags: -d detach, -it interactive TTY, --rm auto-remove, -e KEY=val env, -v vol:/path mount, --network net, --restart unless-stopped, --memory 512m --cpus 1, --user 1000
Dockerfile: FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, ADD, RUN, ENV, ARG, EXPOSE, USER, HEALTHCHECK, ENTRYPOINT ["exec"], CMD ["args"], LABEL, VOLUME
Cache rule: dependency manifests and install before COPY . .; one RUN per logical step with cleanup in the same layer
Multi-stage: FROM x AS builder ... FROM slim; COPY --from=builder /out /app; docker build --target builder for tests
Volumes: docker volume create v | ls | inspect | rm | prune; named volume -v v:/data; bind mount -v $(pwd):/app; tmpfs --tmpfs /run; :ro for read-only
Networks: docker network create net | ls | inspect | connect net c; drivers bridge, host, none, overlay, macvlan; containers resolve each other by name on user-defined networks
Compose: docker compose up -d | down [-v] | ps | logs -f svc | exec svc sh | build | pull | config | up --scale svc=3; files stack with -f, override auto-merged, .env for ${VAR}
Registry: docker login reg | docker tag local reg/org/img:1.0 | docker push reg/org/img:1.0 | pull by digest img@sha256:...
Cleanup: docker system df | docker system prune [-a] [--volumes] | docker container prune | docker builder prune
Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 app error, 125 docker daemon error, 126/127 command not runnable/not found, 137 SIGKILL (OOM), 143 SIGTERM
Security minimum: USER non-root, pin base images, no secrets in ENV/ARG, --cap-drop ALL, never mount docker.sock, scan images in CI
Signals: docker stop = SIGTERM then SIGKILL after 10s; exec-form CMD/ENTRYPOINT so PID 1 is your app; add --init for zombie reaping
